title: Exact directed maximum flow in \(O((m+n) \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge 1\), do there exist a constant \(k\ge 0\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{a}\) that, on every directed graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, m arcs, distinguished distinct vertices s,t and integer capacities in \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{a}\}\), outputs an exact maximum s–t flow with probability at least \(2/3\) in worst-case time \(O((m+n)(\log (n+2))^{k})\)?
definitions: The graph is explicitly given by its labelled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and an arc list, with no loops and at most one arc per ordered vertex pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A flow assigns an integer \(f_{e}\) to each arc, with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing sums at every vertex other than s,t. Its value is the outgoing sum at s minus the incoming sum at s; maximum refers to the largest such value. Output the m flow values, not only an approximate value. Use a word RAM with word length \(B_{a}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed integer \(B_{a}\) large enough to store capacities, total flow and memory addresses. Unit-cost operations are random-access word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division of nonzero divisors. Multiword computations are charged for their component operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed, with each generated word charged. All preprocessing and output are included, and the time bound holds on every random execution. There are no oracles or input-dependent advice. \(A_{a}, k, B_{a}\) and the hidden constant may depend on a, but not on the graph. The \(m+n\) convention includes explicitly listed isolated vertices.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
why: Identify whether exact flow optimization with polynomially bounded capacities admits genuinely polylogarithmic overhead over graph input size.

importance.reason: A central static graph optimization primitive with broad algorithmic consequences. The precise remaining overhead separates the established almost-linear breakthrough from the longstanding nearly linear target; this is a general problem rather than a refinement of one fixed algorithm.

context_blocks.text: Maximum flow is a basic model for routing through capacity constraints. A feasible solution must obey conservation at intermediate vertices, and optimality measures the largest transferable amount between two terminals. Even a graph with small integer capacities can require globally coordinated changes to a feasible routing. The question asks whether finding the exact optimum can cost only a polylogarithmic factor more than reading the graph.

Almost-linear algorithms already represent a major qualitative advance. Chen and coauthors obtained exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow in \(m^{1+o(1)}\) time for polynomially bounded integral data. Li and Wice’s August 2026 preprint obtains an almost-linear maximum-flow bound through a different framework. Neither stated asymptotic guarantee is \(O(m \operatorname{polylog} n)\).

The distinction concerns the remaining overhead. For example, \(\exp (\sqrt{\log  n})\) is subpolynomial in n but exceeds every fixed power of log n. A running time containing that factor can be almost linear without satisfying this card. Removing the residual gap would identify a sharper computational cost for a central graph optimization primitive.

Exactness is also a substantive part of the target. A flow whose value is within a fixed relative error of optimum does not determine the optimum integer value when that value is large. Conversely, restricting capacities to polynomial magnitude means their binary encodings occupy logarithmically many bits each. The question is therefore not asking an algorithm to read arbitrarily long capacities in a graph-size-only time bound.

The primary topic is a static graph algorithm, so the current catalogue places the question in Structural graph theory and graph algorithms. Dynamic maintenance, parallel computation and strong polynomiality for unbounded-bit linear programming impose different requirements. No existing maximum-matching or dynamic-connectivity card represents this flow target.
